slides.say: Given: p squared is smaller than p, which is smaller than r times q, which is smaller than q, which is smaller than r. Which of the following statements is possible but not necessarily true?

Let's read the given chain step by step before checking the choices. First, p squared is smaller than p. p cannot be negative: its square would be positive and larger than p. So p is positive. Squaring it made it smaller, which means p is between zero and one.

Everything to the right of p in the chain is larger than p, so those expressions are positive too. Now look at r times q is smaller than q. q is positive, so divide both sides by q without reversing the inequality. We get r is smaller than one.
So p, q and r are all between zero and one. p is the smallest, and r is the largest.
The question asks for a statement that can be true but is not always true. A statement that is always true is out. A statement that can never be true is out too.

Choice number three compares p times q with p plus q. q is between zero and one, so multiplying p by q makes p smaller. But adding positive q makes p larger. So p times q is always smaller than p plus q. This choice is always true, so it's out.

Choice number one: divide both sides by positive p. The inequality sign stays the same, and we get p times q is smaller than r. p times q is smaller than q, because p is between zero and one. q is smaller than r, so the statement is always true and this choice is out. We can also compare the original products directly. p squared is smaller than p, and q is smaller than r. Both numbers in the left product are smaller than their matches in the right product. So the left product is smaller.
at: p times q is smaller than q

slides.say: Choice number two says p times q is greater than one. Both p and q are positive and smaller than one, so their product is smaller than one too. This statement can never be true, so it's out.

Choice number four says p plus r is smaller than one. We need a case where it works and a case where it fails, while keeping the whole given chain true. Use p is zero point one, q is zero point five, and r is zero point six. The chain holds, and p plus r is zero point seven, smaller than one. Now use p is zero point three, q is zero point eight, and r is zero point nine. The chain still holds, but p plus r is one point two, greater than one. So this statement can be true, but is not always true. Choice number four is our answer. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number four is our answer
